summary:
IGNIS – Interactive Gateway for NASA's Investigative Science is an interactive research platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Flame in Freefall challenge.

NASA has conducted extensive microgravity combustion experiments, but exploring, comparing, and interpreting findings across different investigations can be challenging. IGNIS bridges this gap by transforming NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) experimental data into an accessible, interactive, and evidence-driven research experience.
Our platform features an Interactive Microgravity Laboratory that visualizes liquid- and solid-fuel experimental setups, an intelligent search system for discovering relevant experiments, and a Comparability Guard that highlights differences in experimental conditions. Its Evidence Passport traces observations to original NASA sources, while Scientific Insights provides evidence-grounded answers and identifies limitations when data is insufficient.
IGNIS is designed to help researchers, students, and aerospace engineers explore combustion behavior, understand experimental findings, and identify research gaps relevant to future space exploration.
By combining scientific transparency, interactive visualization, and accessible research tools,IGNIS makes complex microgravity combustion research easier to explore, understand, and responsibly interpret.
details:
IGNIS — Interactive Gateway for NASA's Investigative Science

IGNIS is an interactive, evidence-driven research platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data challenge. Our goal is to make NASA's microgravity combustion research more accessible, understandable, and useful for scientific exploration.

What Does IGNIS Do?

Combustion behaves differently in microgravity, making experimental research essential for understanding fire behavior in space. Although NASA has conducted extensive investigations, exploring experimental records across different datasets and technical documents can be challenging.

IGNIS addresses this problem by bringing selected NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion records into a unified research environment.

The platform integrates data from NASA's Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) and Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) investigations, allowing users to explore solid- and liquid-fuel combustion experiments.

Our key features include:

  • Interactive Microgravity Laboratory: Visualizes combustion experiment setups and allows users to explore qualitative scenarios involving oxygen availability, ambient motion, and sample size.
  • Experiment Explorer: Organizes NASA experimental records for convenient searching and inspection.
  • Intelligent Research Search: Retrieves and ranks relevant experiments using explainable search criteria.
  • Experiment Comparison: Displays experimental measurements side by side and highlights differences in conditions that affect scientific comparability.
  • Evidence Passport: Connects experimental observations to original NASA source references, test identifiers, and recorded fields.
  • Scientific Insights: Provides evidence-grounded answers to research questions while identifying uncertainty and insufficient evidence.

How Does It Work?

IGNIS follows a structured data-processing workflow.

Selected experimental records are collected from NASA's PSI repository, organized into curated datasets, and processed through a Python-based backend. The system validates record structure, preserves original experimental measurements, and exposes the information through REST APIs.

A React-based frontend retrieves these records and presents them through interactive visualizations, searchable experiment tables, comparison tools, and scientific explanations.

Importantly, IGNIS distinguishes between actual NASA measurements and illustrative laboratory animations. Its scientific insights are grounded in available experimental evidence rather than unsupported predictions.

Technologies Used

We developed IGNIS using:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, REST APIs
  • Data Processing: Structured CSV and JSON datasets, validation, and provenance tracking
  • Scientific Intelligence: Evidence-based retrieval, explainable ranking, comparability checks, and deterministic scientific insights
  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub
  • Scientific Data Sources: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), BASS-II, and FLEX

The application was developed using standard computers and web-development tools, without requiring specialized experimental hardware.

Creativity and Innovation

IGNIS goes beyond conventional data dashboards by combining scientific evidence with an interactive learning and research experience.

Instead of presenting isolated measurements, it allows users to understand an experiment's setup, inspect recorded observations, compare related tests, and trace findings back to their original sources.

A distinctive feature is its emphasis on scientific transparency. The Comparability Guard helps prevent misleading interpretations, while Scientific Insights distinguishes supported answers from questions that cannot be resolved using the available evidence.

The interactive laboratory makes complex microgravity combustion concepts more approachable without presenting illustrative visualizations as validated physical simulations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

IGNIS is designed to benefit researchers, students, educators, and aerospace engineers by simplifying access to relevant combustion experiments and supporting more informed scientific exploration.

Its intended impact is to reduce the complexity of navigating experimental research, improve understanding of microgravity combustion behavior, and help users identify meaningful comparisons and research gaps.

These capabilities can contribute to the broader scientific foundation needed for future spacecraft and space-habitat fire-safety research, although IGNIS does not directly predict spacecraft fire hazards or certify material safety.
